passages.title: Going to a Wedding
passages.text: My youngest uncle is getting married. The wedding is in the village. We are all going to the wedding. We are going by train. We are the first to come to the station. My father, my mother, my brother and I. We have one big bag and two small bags. And we have a red water bottle.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Rukmini Banerji
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: How is the family going to the wedding?
question.evidence: We are going by train.
question.explain: The story says, "We are going by train."

passages.title: Goodnight, Tinku!
passages.text: It was a bright moonlit night. All the animals in Mangu's farm were sleeping. Except Tinku! "I am not sleepy, Ma," murmured Tinku. But Ma did not hear him. She was fast asleep. He turned left, and he turned right. He lay on his tummy, and rolled on his back. But he could not sleep!

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Preethi Nambiar
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What is Tinku's problem?
choices: He is too cold at night.
He is too hungry to play.
question.evidence: But he could not sleep!
question.explain: Tinku turned and rolled, but he could not sleep.

passages.title: My Home
passages.text: This is my home. I live here with my whole family. We take off our shoes and chappals here. This is where we wash our face and hands. I hang my clothes on the hook. My grandfather keeps his stick in the corner. We also keep our mats there. My father keeps his motorcycle outside.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Rukmini Banerji
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included. Translated by Manisha Chaudhry.

question.q: What is this story mostly about?
choices: A father who rides his motorcycle
A trip on a train to the village
A grandfather and his old stick
Where a family keeps its things
question.evidence: This is my home. I live here with my whole family.
question.explain: The child shows us the home and where each thing is kept.

passages.title: The Many Tails of Jiril the Squirrel
passages.text: Jiril the squirrel sat on the branch of a tree. He was all alone. Jiril felt lonely. He wished he could play with his friends. He ran down the tree to the ground. He did not find his friends but he did find an acorn to eat. Jiril looked and looked for his friends but he could not find them. He took a nap because he was tired. When Jiril woke up, he decided to climb the tree again. But he was still half asleep and he rolled down to the ground. Soon he found his friends playing and eating. Jiril was happy now as he was not alone.

question.q: Why did Jiril roll down to the ground?
question.evidence: he was still half asleep and he rolled down to the ground
question.explain: Jiril had just woken up, so he was still sleepy.

passages.title: Vayu, the Wind
passages.text: A bolt of lightning far away. Black clouds moving my way. Who makes that happen? Vayu, the Wind! Branches sway and leaves tremble. Flowers gently fall. Who did it all? Vayu, the Wind! Far from the house, we are playing, Yet, I can smell the sweets mother is preparing. Who makes it happen? Vayu, the Wind!

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Madhuri Pai
source.note: Excerpt. Illustrations not included. Translated by Rohini Nilekani.

question.q: Who makes all of these things happen in the poem?
question.evidence: Who makes that happen? Vayu, the Wind!
question.explain: Each part of the poem asks who did it, and the answer is always the wind.

passages.title: Little Painters
passages.text: The painter gave each of them a brush. "Paint the inside of the gate," he said to Veena. "Paint the outside of the gate," he said to Vinay. They picked up two tins of paint and set to work. Veena painted one side of the gate. Vinay painted the other side of the gate.

question.q: Which part of the gate did Vinay paint?
question.evidence: "Paint the outside of the gate," he said to Vinay.
question.explain: The painter told Vinay to paint the outside.

passages.title: The Moon and The Cap
passages.text: All of us went to the Dasara fair. Papa bought Chintu fancy glasses. Mother bought me a bright blue cap. The baby got sugar candy. On the way home, a very strong wind came. It blew my cap away. My cap got stuck on a branch of the old Pipal tree.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Rohini Nilekani
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What made the cap get stuck in the tree?
choices: A very strong wind blew it.
The baby threw it up there.
Chintu tossed it in a game.
question.evidence: a very strong wind came. It blew my cap away.
question.explain: A strong wind blew the cap away and into the tree.

passages.title: Curly and Straight
passages.text: I like straight hair. I like curly hair. I like curly tails. I like straight tails. I like staircases which curl upwards. I like straight staircases. I like the straight road up the hill. I like the road that curls around the hill. I like to draw straight lines... I always draw curly lines...

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Radha HS
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What kind of lines does the child always draw?
question.evidence: I always draw curly lines
question.explain: The child likes straight lines but always draws curly ones.

passages.title: The Boat Ride
passages.text: "Today we shall go on a big boat," said Vikki to Kato. "B... B... But, I... I...am afraid of water, I cannot swim," mumbled Kato. "Come on, you scrappy squirrel! With Vikki around, you need not be afraid. I have been on a boat many times." Vikki importantly leading the way, they reached the river.

question.q: Why is Kato afraid of the boat ride?
question.evidence: I...am afraid of water, I cannot swim
question.explain: Kato is afraid because Kato cannot swim.

passages.title: Rain, Rain
passages.text: A cloud rolled along merrily in the sky. The peacock said, "Why don't you rain? I will dance for you." The fish said, "Please rain. I need more water." The farmer said, "Please rain. I'll plant seeds for the next crop." Raju said, "If you rain, I'll sail paper boats."

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Sanjiv Jaiswal 'Sanjay'
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included. Translated by Manisha Chaudhry.

question.q: What does the peacock say it will do if the cloud rains?
question.evidence: "Why don't you rain? I will dance for you."
question.explain: The peacock promises to dance for the cloud.

passages.title: Chhuk-Chhuk-Chhak
passages.text: Nanhi picked up her slate and chalk. She wanted to draw a long, l-o-n-g train. Nanhi first drew an engine which gave out a lot of smoke, for the long, long train. "Oh dear! Now where shall I make the coaches?" Nanhi wondered, for there was no more space on the slate.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Vinita Krishna
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included. Translated by Ritu Singh.

question.q: Why couldn't Nanhi draw the coaches on her slate?
choices: She forgot how to draw them.
question.evidence: there was no more space on the slate
question.explain: The engine filled the slate, so there was no room left.

passages.title: Up World, Down World
passages.text: Fatima would sit down in the shade of the Arjuna tree and gaze into the leafy Up World. Maa had warned her not to climb the tree's branches. It was safe down below. Fatima didn't know what was in the scary Up World. But that day, Fatima was in for a surprise. As she turned a page, Fatima felt a dull THUMP! on her head. "Ouch!" she yelled, rubbing her sore head. It was a tiny book, barely the size of a pea.

question.q: What fell on Fatima's head?
question.evidence: It was a tiny book, barely the size of a pea.
question.explain: A tiny book, as small as a pea, landed on her head.

passages.title: Bheema, the Sleepyhead
passages.text: Coming back from the river in the evening, Bheema met Moti, the dog. "I can never get up in the morning on time. Will you wake me up?" Bheema asked Moti. "Yes, I will," said Moti and the next morning he barked and barked but did Bheema wake up? No Sir!

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Kiran Kasturia
source.note: Excerpt. Illustrations not included. Translated by Rajesh Khar.

question.q: Did Moti's barking wake Bheema up?
choices: Yes, but he was very cross.
Yes, he woke up right away.
question.evidence: did Bheema wake up? No Sir!
question.explain: Moti barked and barked, but Bheema did not wake up.

passages.title: Goloo the Circle
passages.text: I am Goloo the circle. Everyone likes me. You can find me everywhere, any time! The sun looks like me. When it's too hot, you need an umbrella which also looks like half of me. At night, the moon looks like me with a smile. I look at it through the owl's round eyes.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Jagdish Joshi
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What is Goloo telling us?
choices: Umbrellas keep the hot sun away.
Owls have very big, round eyes.
The moon only comes out at night.
question.evidence: You can find me everywhere, any time!
question.explain: Goloo is a circle, and the sun, moon and owl's eyes are all round.

passages.title: Crocky and friends
passages.text: Crocky the crocodile was sad. He had no friends to play with. Babloo, the butterfly said, "I will play with you, Crocky. Do not cry." Tutoo, the turtle said, "I will play with you, Crocky. Do not cry." Susie, the snake said, "I will also play with you, Crocky. Do not cry." Fred, the frog and Fenny, the fish also came to play. So, Crocky found new friends to play with. He became happy.

question.q: What is this story mostly about?
choices: Crocky gets lost in a pond.
question.evidence: So, Crocky found new friends to play with.
question.explain: Crocky was sad with no friends, then many animals came to play.

passages.title: Under My Bed
passages.text: "What happened dear? Did you call me?" asks Ma. I point towards the tiger. Ma bends and pulls the tiger out from under the bed! Hey, this is no tiger. This is my thick yellow and black sweater. Its buttons shine like a tiger's eyes. I got scared for nothing! Ma gets me some water.

question.q: Why did the child think a tiger was under the bed?
choices: Ma told a story about tigers.
The child heard a loud roar.
A striped cat was hiding under there.
The sweater looked like a tiger.
question.evidence: This is my thick yellow and black sweater. Its buttons shine like a tiger's eyes.
question.explain: The sweater was yellow and black, and its buttons shone like eyes.

passages.title: Saboo and Jojo
passages.text: "Hello! Who are you?" asked a surprised Saboo. "Hello yourself, I am a giraffe. My name is Jojo. I can play with you. If you climb up on to my back, I will take you for a ride." Saboo climbed up and away they went down the road, up the hill, and into town. Saboo shouted happily, "Jojo turn right, now left, and again right," till they came to his friend Munni's house.

question.q: What did Saboo do right after Jojo offered a ride?
choices: He climbed up on Jojo's back.
He went home to his mother.
He went back home to his mother.
question.evidence: Saboo climbed up and away they went
question.explain: Jojo offered a ride, so Saboo climbed up on his back.

passages.title: Aunty Jui's Baby
passages.text: Anu got ready in a jiffy. She gulped down her milk without a fuss. She didn't even cry when her mother combed her hair. The moment Anu entered Aunty's house she shouted, "Aunty! Where is the baby?" "Shhhh..." said Aunty Jui, with her finger on her lips. "Softly. The baby is sleeping." Sleeping? What a bore. Anu began to sulk.

source.name: Pratham Books (StoryWeaver)
source.author: Madhuri Purandare
source.note: Excerpt. Illustrations not included. Translated by Pratham Books Team.

question.q: Anu "got ready in a jiffy." What does "in a jiffy" mean?
question.evidence: Anu got ready in a jiffy.
question.explain: "In a jiffy" means very fast. Anu was in a hurry to see the baby.

passages.title: King of the birds
passages.text: Once long ago, the birds had a meeting. They wanted a king, just like people and animals. Which bird should be king? "The Eagle, he is strong and kingly!" said one. "No, he has no crown, and when he calls, he sounds too sad," said another. "Then Ostrich, because he is the largest and roars like a lion," one called out. "No, he can't fly. The king of the birds must be able to fly."

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: South African Folktale
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: Why did the birds say Ostrich could not be king?
question.evidence: "No, he can't fly. The king of the birds must be able to fly."
question.explain: The birds wanted a king who could fly, and Ostrich can't.

passages.title: Colours of a rainbow
passages.text: A rainbow has seven colours. The first colour is red. Kewyu is wearing a red shirt. The second colour is orange. What else can you see that is the colour orange? The third colour is yellow. The yolk of an egg is yellow. What else can you see that is the colour yellow?

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Caren Echesa
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included. Shortened.

question.q: Which colour comes third in the rainbow?
question.evidence: The third colour is yellow.
question.explain: Red is first, orange is second, and yellow is third.

passages.title: The Race
passages.text: One day the rabbit found a snail. He said to the snail, "You can't run! All you know is how to crawl on the ground." The snail said, "Come on Sunday and you will see." The snail prepared a hundred bits of paper and wrote the same message on them.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Mozambican folktale
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What did the snail get ready?
choices: A big lunch for the Sunday
A map of the race path
question.evidence: The snail prepared a hundred bits of paper
question.explain: The snail made a hundred bits of paper with a message.

passages.title: Keke's swing
passages.text: Keke sat on her swing. She loved her swing. It was the best swing at her school. Keke moved slowly on her swing. Backwards and forwards. Backwards and forwards. When Keke moved, her swing went faster and faster. Soon she was right at the top. Keke looked down at the ground. She was very high up. "Aeei," she called, "Look how high I am!"

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Marion Drew, Khothatso Ranoosi
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What happened when Keke moved on her swing?
question.evidence: her swing went faster and faster
question.explain: Keke moved, and the swing went faster until she was high up.

passages.title: 'M'e Maneo's pumpkin
passages.text: "Stop! You are tickling me," said the pumpkin. "I don't like it." And the pumpkin rolled away down the hill. The pumpkin stopped in a field at the bottom of the hill. Two shepherds found it. "What shall we do with this pumpkin?" they asked. "Let's eat it," they said, "it looks delicious."

question.q: Who found the pumpkin in the field?
question.evidence: Two shepherds found it.
question.explain: Two shepherds found the pumpkin at the bottom of the hill.

passages.title: Lazy Anansi
passages.text: "How will I call you when they're ready?" asked Rabbit. Anansi thought for a minute. "I'll spin a web," he said, "and tie one end around my leg and one end to your pot. When the greens are ready, pull on the web string and I'll come right away." So Anansi tied the web to the pot, and walked on.

question.q: How will Rabbit tell Anansi the greens are ready?
question.evidence: pull on the web string and I'll come right away
question.explain: Anansi tied a web string to the pot for Rabbit to pull.

passages.title: Fox and Rooster
passages.text: There was a time when all the animals lived together as friends. One day they decided to have a meeting to elect a king. Rooster wanted to be king. So he lied to the other animals. He told them, "The red comb on my head is fire! Don't touch the comb on my head!"

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Vincent Afeku
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What did Rooster say his red comb was?
question.evidence: The red comb on my head is fire!
question.explain: Rooster lied and said his comb was fire.

passages.title: A house for Mouse
passages.text: Mouse was looking for a new house. "You can come and sleep with me," said Puppy. "Thank you," said Mouse. That night, Mouse's dreams were bouncy and muddy. "You can come and sleep with me," said Parrot. "Thank you," said Mouse. That night, Mouse's dreams were noisy and wild.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Michele Fry
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included. Shortened.

question.q: Why were Mouse's dreams noisy and wild?
question.evidence: "You can come and sleep with me," said Parrot.
question.explain: Mouse slept with Parrot that night, and Parrot's home is noisy.

passages.title: Tortoise finds his house
passages.text: "Are you looking for something?" Snail asked. "Yes, Snail, I'm looking for my house. Have you seen it, by any chance?" Snail said: "No, I haven't, but I'll help you look!" She climbed onto Tortoise's shell. Tortoise walked on with Snail on his back. They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house. The sun was high in the sky.

question.q: Where did Snail ride while they looked?
choices: On top of a big rock
question.evidence: She climbed onto Tortoise's shell.
question.explain: Snail climbed onto Tortoise's shell to help him look.

passages.title: Friends
passages.text: My name is Simo. I have four friends. Their names are Zizo, Lele, Sisa and Ayanda. My friend Zizo likes to play soccer. My friend Lele likes to swim. My friend Sisa likes to play hide-and-seek. My friend Ayanda likes to read. Me? I like to do all the things they like to do.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Zimbili Dlamini, Hlengiwe Zondi
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What does Lele like to do?
question.evidence: My friend Lele likes to swim.
question.explain: The story says Lele likes to swim.

passages.title: Tell me...now! Colours
passages.text: Why are leaves green? They are not always green. Are they? Why are bananas yellow? Ripe bananas are yellow. Unripe bananas are green. Why are umbrellas black? Not all umbrellas are black. Why is blood red? There is iron in the blood. That makes it red.

question.q: "Unripe bananas are green." What does "unripe" mean?
choices: Very sweet and soft to eat
question.evidence: Ripe bananas are yellow. Unripe bananas are green.
question.explain: Unripe means not ready yet. Bananas turn yellow when they are ripe.

passages.title: Big blue bus
passages.text: Ebei was already dressed when his mother came to wake him. Ebei and his mother walked to the bus stop. They waited for the big blue bus. But the bus did not come. Other people arrived at the bus stop. They complained because the bus was late. "Has the bus left us?" they asked.

question.q: Why did the people at the bus stop complain?
question.evidence: They complained because the bus was late.
question.explain: The people were upset because the bus was late.

passages.title: Disability is Not Inability
passages.text: This is Agnes. She is my teacher. Agnes uses crutches to walk. This is Metobo. He is my favourite radio DJ. Metobo has problems with his eyes. This is Moraa, my neighbour. Moraa is a farmer. Moraa cannot hear. She speaks using Sign Language. This is Osero. He is the best soccer player at my school.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Agnes Mabururu
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: How does Moraa speak with people?
question.evidence: She speaks using Sign Language.
question.explain: Moraa cannot hear, so she speaks using Sign Language.

passages.title: My teacher
passages.text: I love my teacher. She is beautiful. She is a good teacher. She is kind and patient. She has braided her hair very nicely today. She has decorated her hair with colourful beads. Her beads are green, white, red, and yellow. Mom, please would you braid my hair like my teacher's? When I am older I will also put beads in my hair. I will grow up to be just like my teacher!

question.q: What did the teacher put in her hair?
question.evidence: She has decorated her hair with colourful beads.
question.explain: The teacher put colourful beads in her braids.

passages.title: Rats!
passages.text: There was a man who sold oil that he made in his house. And in that house there were rats. Lots of rats! Every day the rats looked at the oil and said, "How can we get that oil?" The rats tried to put their mouths into the bottles. But the spaces in the bottles were too small.

source.name: African Storybook
source.author: Lourenço Magaia Sabão
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: Why couldn't the rats get the oil?
question.evidence: But the spaces in the bottles were too small.
question.explain: The rats' mouths did not fit in the small bottle tops.

passages.title: Zama is great!
passages.text: My little brother sleeps very late. I wake early, because I am great! I am the one who lets in the sun. "You're my morning star," says Ma. I wash myself, I don't need any help. I can cope with cold water and blue smelly soap. Ma reminds, "Don't forget teeth." I reply, "Never, not me!"

source.name: Storybooks Canada
source.author: Michael Oguttu
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: What does Ma call Zama?
question.evidence: "You're my morning star," says Ma.
question.explain: Ma calls Zama her morning star.

passages.title: Hen and Eagle
passages.text: Once upon a time, Hen and Eagle were friends. They lived in peace with all the other birds. None of them could fly. One day, there was famine in the land. Eagle had to walk very far to find food. She came back very tired. "There must be an easier way to travel!" said Eagle.

source.name: Storybooks Canada
source.author: Ann Nduku
source.note: Beginning of the story. Illustrations not included.

question.q: Why did Eagle come back very tired?
choices: She had been flying all day long.
She played games with the other birds.
She had to walk very far for food.
She was building a new nest.
question.evidence: Eagle had to walk very far to find food. She came back very tired.
question.explain: Birds could not fly yet, so Eagle had to walk far.

passages.title: What Vusi's sister said
passages.text: "What have you done?" cried Vusi. "That egg was for a cake. The cake was for my sister's wedding. What will my sister say if there is no wedding cake?" The boys were sorry for teasing Vusi. "We can't help with the cake, but here is a walking stick for your sister," said one. Vusi continued on his journey.

question.q: What did the boys give Vusi for his sister?
question.evidence: here is a walking stick for your sister
question.explain: The boys gave Vusi a walking stick for his sister.

passages.title: Tommy Likes Winter
passages.text: "Not a bit," replied Tommy. "I like winter. I like cold weather. It makes a fellow feel good from the tips of his claws to the tip of his bill. I'm thankful I don't have to take that long journey most of the birds have to. I discovered a secret a long time ago, Peter; shall I tell it to you?"

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why is Tommy thankful?
choices: He doesn't have to make a long trip.
He found lots of seeds to eat today.
He can sing a very pretty song.
He has a warm and cozy nest.
question.evidence: I'm thankful I don't have to take that long journey
question.explain: Tommy likes winter, so he does not have to fly far away like other birds.

passages.title: Reddy's Big Tail
passages.text: "There's one thing I do envy Reddy," spoke up Peter Rabbit, "and that is that big tail of his. It is a wonderful tail. I wish I had one like it."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What does Peter Rabbit wish he had?
question.evidence: I wish I had one like it.
question.explain: Peter wishes he had a big tail like Reddy's.

passages.title: Billy Mink Counts to Three
passages.text: "Now when I count three we'll all dive into the Smiling Pool together and see who can dive the deepest. One!" said Billy Mink. "Two!" said Billy Mink. "Three!" said Billy Mink.

source.name: Old Mother West Wind (Thornton W. Burgess, 1910)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Where will they all dive?
question.evidence: we'll all dive into the Smiling Pool together
question.explain: Billy Mink says they will dive into the Smiling Pool.

passages.title: Paddy the Beaver's Feet
passages.text: "Only my hind feet," said Paddy. "They have webs between the toes just as Honker's have. That is for swimming. But there are no webs between my fingers." He held up a hand for all to see. Sure enough, the fingers were free.

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What are the webs on Paddy's hind feet for?
question.evidence: That is for swimming.
question.explain: The webs between his toes help Paddy swim.

passages.title: Teacher's Hidden Nest
passages.text: Teacher's eyes twinkled. "I guess it won't do any harm to tell you that much," said he. "No, it isn't in a tree. It is on the ground and, if I do say it, it is as well hidden a nest as anybody can build. Oh, Peter, watch your step! Watch your step!" Teacher fairly shrieked this warning.

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: "Teacher fairly shrieked this warning." What does "shrieked" mean?
question.evidence: Teacher fairly shrieked this warning.
question.explain: To shriek is to cry out in a loud, high voice.

passages.title: Whitefoot Likes the Night
passages.text: "I don't," replied Whitefoot. "I sleep most of the time during the day, and work and play at night. I feel safer then. But on dull days I often come out. It is the bright sunlight I don't like. That is one reason I stick to the Green Forest. I don't see how Cousin Danny stands it out there on the Green Meadows."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: When does Whitefoot work and play?
question.evidence: work and play at night
question.explain: Whitefoot sleeps in the day and works and plays at night.

passages.title: Why Come South?
passages.text: "If you are so fond of the cold in the Far North, the snow and the ice, what did you come south at all for? Why don't you stay up there all the year around?" demanded Peter.

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: What does Peter say his friend is fond of?
question.evidence: If you are so fond of the cold in the Far North, the snow and the ice
question.explain: Peter says his friend is fond of the cold, the snow and the ice.

passages.title: Prickly Porky in Winter
passages.text: "What should I sleep for?" grumbled Prickly Porky. "Cold weather doesn't bother me. I like it. I have the Green Forest pretty much to myself then. I like to be alone. And as long as there are trees, there is plenty to eat. I sleep a great deal in the daytime because I like night best."

source.name: The Burgess Animal Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1920)
source.author: Thornton W. Burgess

question.q: Why doesn't Prickly Porky need to sleep all winter?
choices: He lives in a warm, cozy cave.
He stores lots of nuts for later.
question.evidence: Cold weather doesn't bother me.
question.explain: Prickly Porky says cold weather doesn't bother him, and trees give him food.

passages.title: Jenny Wren and Snake Skins
passages.text: "Snake skins! Snake skins!" shrieked Jenny Wren. "What are you talking about, Peter Rabbit? I never have anything to do with Snake skins and don't want to. Ugh! It makes me shiver just to think of it."

source.name: The Burgess Bird Book for Children (Thornton W. Burgess, 1919)

passages.title: The Wasp Sting
passages.text: "The wasp too, then?" asked Jules. "One stung me once when I tried to drive it from a bunch of grapes. I did not say anything, but all the same I was not very comfortable. To think that such a tiny thing can hurt one so! It seemed as if my hands were on fire."
